client: I've been feeling so much pressure to keep my GPA perfect this year, especially after getting that C in calculus last semester. I know it's just one grade, but I can't stop thinking about how it might ruin my chances for grad school or internships. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help since the pressure isn't going away - the expectations are still there.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of expectations, and that one grade seems to have become magnified in your mind. I notice you mentioned doubting whether talking will help—would you be willing to explore what makes the pressure feel so unshakable right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess the pressure feels unshakable because I’ve always tied my worth to my grades. If I don’t do well, I feel like I’m failing everyone—my parents, my teachers, even myself. Talking about it helps a little, but I’m not sure it’ll change how I feel deep down.
therapist: I hear how deeply connected your sense of self-worth is to academic performance—that must feel incredibly heavy to carry. Let's gently examine whether "failing everyone" is a thought we might test against reality, or if there might be other ways to measure your worth beyond grades.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I know grades aren't everything, but they feel like the only concrete proof that I'm not a disappointment. When I get anything less than an A, it's like my brain automatically goes to "See? You're failing at life." I want to believe there's more to me than grades, but that belief feels so abstract compared to the immediate punch in the gut when I see a bad score.
therapist: You're describing such a vivid and painful automatic reaction—that immediate "punch in the gut" when grades don't meet your expectations. I notice you're speaking with a lot of energy about this—would it be helpful to explore what physical sensations or emotions arise in that moment when you see a disappointing score?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I get this sinking feeling in my stomach when I see a bad grade. My chest gets tight too, and my mind immediately jumps to thoughts like "I'll never be good enough" or "Everyone must think I'm stupid." It's hard to shake those feelings even when I know I studied hard. Sometimes I think maybe I'm just not cut out for this program, even though that's probably not true.
therapist: The physical sensations and automatic thoughts you're describing—the sinking stomach, tight chest, and those immediate judgments—sound overwhelming in those moments. I wonder if we could slow down that experience together to examine whether those bodily reactions might be amplifying the harshness of your self-judgments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I know you're trying to help, but when my chest gets tight like that, it's hard to even think straight. The thoughts just flood in - "You're failing," "Everyone can tell you're freaking out" - and trying to examine them in the moment feels impossible. It's like trying to read a book during an earthquake.
therapist: Your description of trying to read during an earthquake is so vivid—it really captures how overwhelming those moments feel. When those thoughts flood in, do you notice if there's a particular physical sensation that comes first, or does it all seem to happen at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It all kind of happens at once, honestly. My chest gets tight, and my heart starts racing, and then the thoughts just flood in—like, "What if it’s worse than last time?" or "What if I’m not prepared?" It’s hard to pinpoint what starts first because it feels like everything crashes together. I’m not sure if that makes sense, but it’s like my body and mind are on the same chaotic wavelength.
therapist: You're describing such an intense wave of physical and mental reactions—it sounds completely overwhelming when they all crash together like that. Would it be helpful to explore how this experience might be different if we could find even a small pause between the physical sensations and those flooding thoughts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if finding a pause would really help—when I'm in that state, everything feels like it's happening all at once. My heart races and my thoughts spiral about everything I should be doing or should have done better, and it's like my body and brain are screaming at the same time. Even when people tell me to just breathe, it feels impossible to separate any of it.
therapist: It sounds like those moments feel completely consuming—like your body and mind are locked in this overwhelming cycle together. When people suggest simply breathing, does that ever feel dismissive of how intense the experience actually is for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Yeah, it does feel dismissive when people tell me to just breathe. It’s like they don’t understand how paralyzing it is—like I’m stuck in this storm and breathing feels impossible. I want to believe it could help, but in the moment, it just doesn’t feel like enough to calm the chaos in my head.
therapist: I hear how deeply frustrating it feels when well-meaning advice misses the mark of your actual experience—like being told to breathe when you're stuck in that paralyzing storm. Would it feel more helpful if we explored what small action might feel possible in those moments, even if it's not the "perfect" calming technique?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess I'm just tired of people acting like there's some magic trick to make the anxiety go away. Even small actions feel impossible when I'm in that state—like my brain just shuts down. I don't know if anything would help in those moments, honestly.
therapist: I hear how exhausting it feels to be told there's a simple fix when your experience feels anything but simple—it sounds like you're craving understanding more than solutions. When you say your brain shuts down, does it feel like it's protecting you in some way, even though it's overwhelming?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client:
Yeah, I guess my brain does try to protect me in a weird way. When things get too overwhelming, it's like everything just goes blank—like hitting a pause button. But then I feel guilty afterward because I can't handle normal situations that other people seem to manage fine. 

It’s frustrating because part of me wants to push through, but another part is scared of what might happen if I actually let myself feel everything. Do you think that makes sense? Or does it just sound like I’m making excuses?
therapist: It sounds like you're noticing two conflicting parts of yourself—one that wants to push through and another that’s understandably cautious about feeling overwhelmed. Does the guilt you feel afterward come from comparing yourself to others, or is it more about your own expectations of how you "should" handle things?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
